summaries.example: Imagine a person who knows every true answer in a giant library. Now add questions about what people feel, what happened yesterday, and what may happen tomorrow. Philosophers ask whether knowing a future choice would make that choice no longer free. Some say knowledge does not force the choice; others think the problem is harder.
summaries.summary: Omniscience means complete or maximum knowledge. In discussions of God, it is often defined as knowing every true proposition. Philosophers debate whether this also requires never believing anything false, being unable to lose omniscience, or knowing the experiences of every conscious person. The hardest traditional question concerns future free actions. If God already knows that someone will do something, does that person still choose freely? One response says that knowing an action does not cause it. Another says that facts about the past, including an earlier divine belief, may seem unable to be changed, creating a problem for freedom. Some philosophers answer by saying that God is outside ordinary time, while others limit divine knowledge of future free choices. The entry also examines whether an unchanging God could know changing truths, whether God can know someone else’s first-person perspective, whether omniscience includes direct knowledge of particular things, and whether there is a total collection of all truths. These debates show that the simple idea of “knowing everything” raises many questions about time, choice, truth, and different kinds of knowledge.
key_ideas: Omniscience is usually described as knowing every truth.
Some philosophers add that an all-knowing being must never believe anything false.
A major puzzle asks whether God’s knowledge of future human actions leaves room for free choice.
Other puzzles concern change over time, knowing another person’s point of view, and whether there can be one collection containing every truth.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because it connects ideas people often hold together: a perfect God, guidance of the world, and human responsibility. Thinking carefully about omniscience helps us notice that “knowing,” “causing,” “choosing,” and “being in time” may not mean the same thing. It also teaches a useful philosophy habit: test a big definition by asking whether it works in unusual cases.

important_terms.definition: Knowing everything that is true, or having the greatest possible knowledge.
A statement or claim that is true or false, such as “The bell rang.”
The ability to choose and act without being forced in the relevant way.
Knowledge about what will happen later.
A way of thinking about God as caring for and guiding events in the world.

questions_to_think_about: If someone knows what you will choose, does that person make you choose it?
Can a person know a fact without thinking about it at that moment?
Is knowing that “Maya is in the hospital” the same as Maya knowing “I am in the hospital”?
Does a perfect being need to know every kind of truth in exactly the same way?

summaries.example: Suppose that yesterday God knew with certainty that Jordan will volunteer tomorrow. A familiar argument says: the past is fixed; God’s past belief cannot now be changed; and that belief entails that Jordan volunteers. Therefore Jordan cannot do otherwise and is not free. Critics challenge different steps. They may distinguish a necessary connection between the belief and the action from the action’s being necessary in itself, argue that some past-looking facts also depend on later events, or deny that inability to change the past removes freedom.
summaries.summary:
The SEP entry treats omniscience as a philosophical account of divine knowledge rather than as a general theological application. The usual definition is: for every true proposition, an omniscient subject knows that proposition. Some accounts add that the subject knows which propositions are false or believes no falsehoods; others restrict omniscience when complete knowledge would conflict with other divine attributes. Philosophers also ask whether divine knowledge is infallible, necessary, conscious at every moment, or reached by inference.

The central historical problem concerns foreknowledge and free action. If God knows in advance that a person will perform an action, an argument appears to show that the action is unavoidable. The argument relies on claims about fixed past facts and the transmission of a special kind of necessity through entailment. Replies attack each stage: they distinguish necessity of a conditional from necessity of its outcome, question whether divine-belief reports are purely past facts, or deny that inability to alter the past rules out freedom. Other views hold that God’s eternal perspective is not temporal foreknowledge, or that omniscience does not include truths about future free actions. These positions have implications for providence, since guidance of the world may seem to require knowledge of what free agents will do.

Further puzzles concern whether changing truths require a changing knower, whether God can possess another person’s first-person knowledge, and whether omniscience includes de re knowledge of every individual and property. Finally, a Cantorian argument challenges the existence of a set of all truths. A reply separates the existence of such a set from the intelligibility of knowing every truth. The entry presents these
key_ideas: The standard definition says that if a proposition is true, an omniscient being knows it. Alternative definitions add knowledge that propositions are false or exclude false beliefs.
Omniscience may be supplemented by infallibility, essential omniscience, non-discursive awareness, or knowledge that is not divided into ordinary beliefs.
The foreknowledge argument depends on disputed claims about the necessity of the past, entailment, and whether a person can have power over what would have been true earlier.

Responses include distinguishing kinds of necessity, appealing to divine eternity, limiting knowledge of future free actions, and defending forms of human ability involving counterfactual dependence on the past.
Indexical and first-person knowledge create further problems: knowing that a person is in the hospital is not obviously the same as knowing “I am in the hospital.”
A set-theoretic argument says there cannot be a set of all truths, but critics argue that knowing every truth need not require such a set.
summaries.why_it_matters: Omniscience matters because it tests how several major concepts fit together: perfection, providence, time, truth, knowledge, and freedom. The debates also model careful argument analysis. Rather than asking only whether a conclusion sounds plausible, philosophers identify the exact definition and examine each premise, especially when ordinary words such as “necessary,” “knows,” and “can” hide different meanings.

important_terms.definition: The property of having complete or maximal knowledge, commonly formulated as knowledge of every true proposition.
A claim that can be true or false and can be an object of knowledge or belief.
Knowledge of truths about the future.
A kind of necessity associated with the unalterability of the past; philosophers disagree about how it transfers to later events.
Knowledge of a fact from a particular first-person standpoint, such as knowing that I am in the hospital.
Knowledge concerning a particular object as having a property or standing in a relation, rather than merely knowing a general description.
The view that a being cannot possibly fail to be omniscient. It is stronger than merely being omniscient now.
The claim that there is a set containing every truth. A Cantorian argument challenges whether such a set exists.

questions_to_think_about: Does certainty about an action show that the action is caused or that it is not free?
Is the statement “God believed yesterday that Jordan will act tomorrow” wholly about the past?
Could one person know another person’s first-person experience without having that experience?
Should a definition of omniscience include knowledge of particular objects and perspectives, not just true propositions?
Does the impossibility of a set of all truths imply that no being can know every truth?

summaries.example: Suppose your teacher somehow knows that you will choose chocolate ice cream after school. Did the teacher’s knowledge make you choose chocolate? One philosopher might say no: knowing what happens is different from causing it. Another might ask whether, if the teacher’s belief was already true yesterday, you can still choose vanilla today. Philosophers try to find which part of this reasoning is mistaken or whether future free choices should be left unknown.
summaries.summary:
Omniscience is usually understood as knowing every truth. A proposition is simply a claim that can be true or false. Philosophers of religion ask whether this basic definition is enough. Perhaps an omniscient being must also know that false claims are false, never believe a false claim, or possess knowledge in a special perfect way. Some discussions add knowledge of every conscious person’s inner point of view, sometimes described as perfect awareness of subjective experience.

The most famous problem involves foreknowledge and free action. If God knows today that a person will perform an action tomorrow, it may seem that the person cannot avoid doing it. If the person cannot avoid it, the action may not be free. But the argument can be challenged. “It is necessary that if God knows the action, it happens” is different from “if God knows the action, then the action is necessary.” Also, philosophers disagree about whether statements reporting God’s earlier beliefs are simply fixed past facts. Some defend an eternal divine viewpoint, while others say that future free actions are not yet truths available to be known, or are known only in limited ways. These choices affect views about providence, the idea that God directs or cares for events.

The entry also considers whether an unchanging God can know truths that change as time passes, whether God can know another person’s “I” perspective, and whether complete knowledge includes direct knowledge of particular things. A more technical objection argues that there cannot be a set containing every truth. Critics reply that knowing every truth may not require such a set. Overall, the entry shows why a seemingly simple idea—knowing everything—leads to debates about language, time, freedom, and mathematics.
key_ideas: The usual view defines omniscience as knowing every true proposition.
Some philosophers think omniscience should also include never having a false belief or being unable to lose one’s all-knowing status.
The main disagreement is whether knowledge of future choices conflicts with human freedom.
Some thinkers say God’s knowledge is eternal rather than knowledge of the future in the ordinary time-based sense.
Other proposals limit knowledge of future free actions, while still allowing knowledge of possibilities or probabilities.
Questions about changing facts, personal viewpoints, particular objects, and the totality of truths make the simple definition more complicated.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it asks whether important ideas about God and human life can fit together consistently. It also helps readers practice separating knowledge from cause, and certainty from necessity. Those distinctions are useful far beyond philosophy of religion: they apply whenever people reason about predictions, responsibility, time, and what someone can or cannot do.

important_terms.definition: A statement that can be true or false and can be known or believed.
Knowing something about a later time before that time arrives.
The idea that a past fact is settled and cannot be changed now.
A choice or action that is not forced and is made freely in the relevant sense.
Knowing something from one’s own point of view, especially knowing “I” am a certain person or place.

questions_to_think_about: Does knowing an event guarantee it, or only accurately describe what will happen?
Can a fact about the past include information about a later event?
Is knowing that Alex is in a room different from Alex knowing “I am in the room”?
Would a being need to think about every truth all at once to know everything?
Can “all truths” exist as one enormous collection?
